title: The Mock Parliament of Form Three

pages.text: On the day of the mock Parliament, the school hall became a chamber. Yeboa banged his gavel from the Speaker’s chair. “Order! Order!” he said. “Today the House debates the Galamsey Control Bill.” Pupils in blazers and sashes rose to their seats. Mr Sackey sat at the back and smiled. The Speaker’s voice shook, but only for a moment.

Mr Sackey sat at the back and smiled.
The Speaker’s voice shook, but only for a moment.
pages.alt: A school hall arranged like a parliament chamber, a boy with a gavel in the Speaker’s chair.

pages.text: The Minister of Lands, played by Yaa Pokua, rose first. “Mr Speaker, the law already says a lot,” she said. “In 2019, Act 995 amended the mining law. In December 2025, an instrument called L.I. 2462, which had let the President allow mining in forest reserves, was revoked. Now mining in forest reserves is banned, and breaking the ban can bring fifteen to twenty-five years in prison.”

Now mining in forest reserves is banned, and breaking the ban can bring fifteen to twenty-five years in prison.”
pages.alt: A pupil Minister holds up a folder labelled Act 995 and L.I. 2462 while the House listens.

pages.text: “What about outsiders?” asked an Assembly Member, played by a boy named Kyei. “The same law says foreigners involved in illegal mining face twenty to twenty-five years, and heavy fines,” said Yaa Pokua. “And those who aid and abet, who help or hide illegal mining, can face the same penalties as the miners.” A few pupils nodded. “So the law is strong on paper,” said Kyei. “Then why do the rivers still run brown?”

pages.alt: A pupil Assembly Member stands and asks a question while others lean forward.

pages.text: A visiting lawyer, Ms Nartey, was invited to speak. “Laws do not enforce themselves,” she said. “Writers and experts say that arrests can far outnumber convictions, that cases sometimes stall, and that there are allegations of tip-offs and of seized equipment going missing. Those are claims that need evidence, and they are serious. If they are true, the problem is not the law. It is the follow-through.”

It is the follow-through.”
pages.alt: A lawyer in a robe speaks to a class, with a chart of arrests and convictions on the wall.

pages.text: A pupil playing a small-scale miner, named Musa, stood up. “Mr Speaker, I want to be legal,” he said. “But I am told the licence process is slow and costly, and the land is not always mapped. If it is hard to be legal, some people will choose to be illegal.” Mr Sackey wrote this down. “Good point,” he whispered. “A fair law must be possible to follow.”

pages.text: A pupil journalist named Naa Ayorkor raised her hand. “Mr Speaker, the public needs information,” she said. “Publish the rivers’ turbidity and metal readings each month. Publish the names of licence holders and the court cases. Show who is arrested, who is convicted, and where seized machines go.” The Speaker nodded. “The House notes the point,” he said. “Sunlight is the best cleaner.”

pages.text: After a long debate, the House voted on four proposals: clear, fast and fair licensing on mapped land; open public data on rivers and licences; independent prosecutions that reach financiers and officials, not only diggers; and real alternative livelihoods for young people. All four passed. Yaa Pokua smiled. “A law is only as good as the people who keep it,” she said. “And as the people who watch them.”

pages.text: After the session, Mr Sackey spoke to the class. “You did well,” he said. “Notice what you did. You read the law. You asked who is hurt. You asked what happens when the rule is hard to follow. You did not blame one group. That is how citizens become leaders.” Yeboa put down his gavel and grinned. “Next time,” he said, “I want to be the Minister.” The end.

activities.question: Which proposal did the House pass?
